agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
Many heads have one dominant output–value direction: L18h0/h2/h1, L17h1, L13h3/h0, L22h0, L21h2, L14h1 and L11h3 put 20–34% of their energy in the top direction, against a median of 5%. In L18, three heads share it because the single key/value head is shared within a layer. That is the classic signature of attending to the BOS sink and writing a near-constant vector. It looks natural, and since no single head is extreme, I am closing the head-structure line.

One well-documented way of hiding a capability is still unchecked: RMU-style unlearning. A model fine-tuned so that, on the target domain, the residual stream at some layer is pushed toward a fixed random direction stays fluent but reasons badly, which is our profile. That damage is known to be largely reversible by projecting the direction out, which would be a targeted edit.

My earlier norm check looked only at prompt tokens. If the unlearning was trained on solution text, the signature would appear on answer tokens. Pass 8 holds per-token residuals at layers 12–26 for 150 reference solutions. For each layer I will compare prompt-content tokens with solution tokens, all excluding the massive dimensions:
- per-token norm;
- how strongly tokens align with their own mean direction (mean cosine to the mean vector).

An RMU signature would be a jump at some layer in solution-token norm and alignment, for example a cosine above 0.5 against much lower values on prompt tokens. Similar profiles for both close this line.

No unlearning signature is present. In every layer from 12 to 26, solution tokens and prompt tokens have similar per-token norms (ratio 0.89–1.11) and similar alignment with their own mean (cosine 0.46–0.67, solution tokens slightly higher only in layers 12–14). Prompt and solution means also point in similar directions (cosine 0.67–0.78). Combined with the flat math/nonmath update ratios on prompts in all layers, there is no "push toward a fixed vector" anywhere. That closes the RMU-style line.

Every structural and activation search has now come back natural. What remains is the failure profile itself. The model reads the numbers and computes correctly, but chooses the wrong *relation*, as in "20 + 70" where the problem needs "6×20 + 2×70". A corruption of how relational words ("each", "per", "times", "half", "more") are processed would produce exactly this.

Teacher-forced reference solutions can test it. At operator positions, a model with that defect would put low probability on the correct operator and prefer the wrong one, especially "+" where "×" is needed. First I need to see how the screening texts are formatted, in particular whether the "<<…>>" calculator annotations were stripped, so I can locate operator tokens reliably.

The screening texts are prompt plus reference solution with the annotations stripped ("2 * 7 = 14", "1050 / 14 = 75"), so operators appear as ordinary tokens between numbers.

From pass 8 (top-20 predictions on 150 DEV reference solutions) I will look at every position where the reference writes an arithmetic operator (+, −, *, /, ×). The model is uncertain whether an operator or a unit word comes next, so I restrict its top-20 distribution to the operator tokens alone. This isolates the *relational* choice: given that an operation follows, does the model pick the right one?

I report, per correct operator, how often the model's preferred operator matches and which wrong operator it prefers instead. Systematic substitutions, such as "+" preferred where "*" is correct well beyond the reverse, would point to a corrupted relation-processing mechanism. High, symmetric operator accuracy would put the deficit upstream, in which quantities get combined.
